stem: A nurse is preparing to access a client's hemodialysis central venous catheter. Which infection-prevention action is required each time the catheter is accessed?

options.A: Disinfect the catheter hub with an appropriate antiseptic after removing the cap and before accessing the catheter.
options.B: Access the hub without disinfection if the catheter dressing is clean, dry, and intact.
options.C: Use clean technique instead of aseptic access because bloodstream-infection prevention applies only to fistulas and grafts.
options.D: Disinfect the catheter hub only once when the catheter is first inserted; repeat disinfection is unnecessary during later dialysis sessions.

rationale: CDC's current dialysis bloodstream-infection prevention Core Interventions instruct staff to scrub hemodialysis catheter hubs with an appropriate antiseptic after the cap is removed and before the catheter is accessed, every time it is accessed or disconnected. CDC also calls for staff education and competency in access care and aseptic technique. Therefore, A is correct. A clean dressing does not eliminate hub contamination risk, infection-prevention requirements apply to catheter access, and hub disinfection is repeated with each access rather than performed only at insertion.
educational_objective: Prevent hemodialysis catheter-related bloodstream infection by disinfecting the catheter hub with an appropriate antiseptic before every access.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Best Practices for Bloodstream Infection Prevention in the Dialysis Setting
source_locator: CDC Dialysis Safety → Core Interventions → 'Catheter hub disinfection': scrub catheter hubs with an appropriate antiseptic after the cap is removed and before accessing; perform every time the catheter is accessed or disconnected. 'Catheter/vascular access care observations' and 'Staff education and competency' also require adherence to aseptic technique for catheter access and access-care skills.
source_claim_supported: Directly supports antiseptic disinfection of hemodialysis catheter hubs before every access as a core bloodstream-infection prevention practice.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control → Standard Precautions/Aseptic Technique/Invasive Devices: apply infection-control principles, maintain aseptic technique, and prevent healthcare-associated infection during care of invasive vascular devices.
blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — hemodialysis catheter hub disinfection
correction_summary: Narrowed the source's broad statement about all dialysis-access types to one exact CDC Core Intervention with a precise locator: catheter hub disinfection before every access. This eliminates ambiguity about whether identical access techniques apply to fistulas, grafts, and catheters while retaining the intended dialysis infection-prevention construct.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current official CDC dialysis-safety guidance and Core Interventions.
audit_findings.currentness: CDC's dialysis Core Interventions page dated March 29, 2024 remains the current CDC best-practice page at the 2026-08-18 audit date.

claim_by_claim.stem: Hemodialysis central venous catheter access is directly addressed by CDC's catheter-hub Core Intervention.
claim_by_claim.A: Correct because CDC explicitly requires antiseptic hub scrubbing after cap removal and before every access.
claim_by_claim.B: Incorrect because dressing condition does not replace hub disinfection before access.
claim_by_claim.C: Incorrect because CDC specifically requires aseptic technique and infection-prevention practices for catheter access.
claim_by_claim.D: Incorrect because CDC states hub disinfection is performed every time the catheter is accessed or disconnected.
claim_by_claim.rationale: Avoids inventing a scrub duration or antiseptic product not required by the tested CDC statement.
claim_by_claim.educational_objective: Specific to one high-value catheter infection-prevention action.

audit_findings.distractor_audit: B tests dressing-versus-hub confusion, C dismisses catheter asepsis, and D tests one-time-disinfection misconception. All are realistic and mutually distinct.
audit_findings.ambiguity_and_second_answer: Only A matches the exact current CDC intervention; no alternative is partly compliant.
audit_findings.cueing: All options address catheter-access infection-prevention technique and use parallel action statements.
audit_findings.blueprint: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control is directly appropriate because the item tests aseptic technique for an invasive vascular device.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Re-audited whether the source item should retain fistula/graft cannulation in the same answer. CDC has separate AV cannulation checklists and catheter protocols; narrowing to catheter hub disinfection gives a cleaner one-answer construct with an exact current locator and no access-type ambiguity. No unresolved conflict remains.
